doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Racial mixing in New York music and the move west
summary: Musicians mixed freely until a shift toward separation late in his New York years; he moved to Los Angeles in the early 1960s.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So the racial scene between musicians was cool?
Yeah. Really cool. There wasn’t too much static like we can’t come to our part of town or else it’s a little uncool you know. There was more movement going on.
Did it change while you were still in New York?

No I think it changed at the end of when I was in New York. It just seemed to be a little bit more, what do you call it, the opposite thing, like where before everybody kind of blended together and you could work together. Now they tended toward all-black and then all-white. Not everybody.
You moved to Los Angeles when?
While the Civil Rights movement was getting going, and I guess there was a certain amount of black power type things? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
